title: Grouping with Canonical Keys
summary: Mapping items into groups keyed by a computed signature — Group Anagrams, custom canonical keys, and telling a grouping problem apart from a counting one.

slides.markdown:
[frequency-counting-patterns](frequency-counting-patterns) counts occurrences of raw values. **Grouping** is the closely related but distinct move: instead of counting, you bucket items together under a computed **signature** — a value derived from each item such that items belonging together produce the identical signature.

Group Anagrams is the canonical example: `"eat"`, `"tea"`, and `"ate"` are different strings but the same signature (their sorted letters, or their letter-count tuple), so they land in the same group.

The hashmap's role shifts one more time: a set answered "is it here," a frequency table answered "how many," and a grouping map answers "which bucket does this belong to" — key is the signature, value is a growing list of everything that shares it.

slides.subTitle: A hashmap of key to list of items
A sorted string as the canonical key
Correctness and cost
slides.markdown:
| | Sorted-string key | 26-count-tuple key |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness | Correct for any alphabet | Correct only if the alphabet is known and fixed |
| Cost per string (length m) | O(m log m) to sort | O(m) to count, O(26) to build the tuple |
| Key type | A string — directly hashable | A tuple of counts — hashable if the language supports tuple hashing |
| Scales with alphabet size | No — sorting cost is independent of alphabet | Yes — a 256-count tuple for bytes, impractical for full Unicode |

For lowercase-English-only anagrams, the count-tuple key is asymptotically better — O(m) beats O(m log m) — and is the answer to give if asked to optimize past the sorted-string solution. For an unconstrained alphabet, the sorted string is both simpler and more broadly correct, since a fixed-size tuple stops being fixed-size once the alphabet isn't bounded.

slides.subTitle: Custom groupings — digit sum, shape, remainder
slides.markdown:
The general skill: given "group these items by X," find a signature that is (a) cheap to compute and (b) provably identical for exactly the items that should share a group — no false positives, no false negatives.

A few worked examples of the same shape:

- **Group numbers by digit sum** — signature is `sum(int(d) for d in str(n))`.
- **Group points by whether they lie on the same line through the origin** — signature is the reduced slope as a fraction `(dy/gcd, dx/gcd)`, not a raw float (floats introduce precision errors that break equality).
- **Group numbers by remainder mod k** — signature is simply `n % k`.
- **Group intervals that overlap** — this one does *not* reduce to a simple signature; overlap isn't an equivalence relation in the same way (A overlaps B and B overlaps C doesn't mean A overlaps C), so it needs a different technique (sorting plus merging), not grouping by key.

That last example is the important caution: not every "put similar things together" question is a grouping problem. Grouping requires the similarity to be a true equivalence — reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

slides.subTitle: Over a single scan of the input
slides.markdown:
Watching the map build up makes the pattern concrete: each new item either creates a new bucket (first time its signature is seen) or appends to an existing one (signature already present) — never anything else.

slides.subTitle: Using a mutable list or an unhashable type as a key
slides.markdown:
A signature must be **hashable** to key a map with it — in Python that rules out lists and dicts directly (`unhashable type: 'list'`), a common trip-up when the natural signature is "a list of counts."

The fix is nearly always to convert to an immutable, hashable equivalent before using it as a key: a list of counts becomes a **tuple** of counts; a set of tags becomes a **frozenset**; a mutable custom object needs an immutable value type (or a manually defined, stable hash) rather than being keyed on directly.

```python
counts = [0] * 26            # unhashable
key = tuple(counts)          # hashable — use this as the map key
```

This is the same underlying hazard as [mutable keys breaking lookups](hash-table-mechanics) in a plain hashmap — a signature that can change after being used as a key produces exactly the same silent-miss bug, just dressed up as a grouping problem instead of a lookup one.

slides.subTitle: Recognizing which one the question is really asking for
slides.markdown:
| | Counting (frequency table) | Grouping (canonical key) |
|---|---|---|
| Map value | An integer count | A list of the original items |
| Answers | "How many of X" | "Which items belong with X" |
| Typical question phrasing | "most frequent," "count of" | "group by," "cluster," "same X as" |
| Loses original items? | Yes — only the count survives | No — every original item is preserved |

The fastest way to tell them apart while reading a prompt: if the expected output needs the **original items back** (a list of anagram groups, not just how many groups exist), it's grouping. If the output is a number or a single representative value (a count, a max, a majority element), it's counting. Misreading a grouping question as a counting one loses the actual items the answer needs to return.

slides.sectionTitle: When the signature itself is the expensive part
slides.markdown:
The hashmap side of grouping is always O(n) — one insert per item. What actually determines the total complexity is almost always **how expensive the signature computation is per item**, not the grouping mechanism itself.

Sorting each string for Group Anagrams (O(m log m) per string) dominates over the O(1) amortized map insert. Computing a reduced-fraction slope for collinear points needs a gcd computation per pair. A custom signature involving, say, a recursive structural hash of a tree needs its own complexity accounting entirely separate from the O(n) grouping loop around it.

When asked for the complexity of a grouping solution, the correct answer is always **(cost to compute one signature) × n**, plus the O(n) (or O(n log n) if the grouping itself needs sorted output) for the map operations — naming both parts separately is what shows you're not just pattern-matching "grouping problem, therefore O(n)."

The tell for a grouping problem: the prompt says "group," "cluster," or "same as," and the expected output is a collection of collections — not a single number.

The recipe is always: design a signature that is a true equivalence relation for the grouping you want, make sure it's hashable, then run the one-line group-by loop. Where the real thinking happens is designing the signature — the loop itself never changes.

The next topic in this group moves from grouping (bucketing by an exact signature) to a different hashmap trick entirely: using a **running prefix sum** as the key, which turns subarray-sum questions into the same one-pass-plus-map shape once more, this time keyed by an accumulating value rather than a fixed signature.
